conceptTag: Amazon gets paid before it pays
readerTitle: How Amazon's customers helped pay for its growth
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Amazon, 초기 온라인 서점 시절과 마켓플레이스) + 가상 적용 (주문 제작 철제 선반 공장). 결제 타이밍 그림은 설명용 예시이며 Amazon의 실제 일수가 아님
insight: 고객이 먼저 돈을 내고 공급업체에는 나중에 지불하는 구조라면, 성장은 현금을 먹는 게 아니라 현금을 만들어 낸다. 성장이 현금에 좋은지 나쁜지는 결제 순서가 정한다.
misconception: 빨리 성장하는 회사는 반드시 외부 자금이 더 필요하고, 장부상 적자면 현금도 곧 바닥난다.

sources.text: Amazon.com 1997 Letter to Shareholders and 1997 IPO prospectus (early business model, card payments at order)
Jeff Bezos, 2004 Letter to Shareholders (free cash flow per share as Amazon's 'ultimate financial measure')
Amazon.com Form 10-K filings, 2002 and 2003 (annual net loss in 2002, net income in 2003)
Amazon Seller Central help pages on disbursement schedules for third-party sellers

factChecks.note: '2003년에야 첫 연간 흑자'는 Amazon 10-K(2002년 순손실, 2003년 순이익)로 확인하세요. 분기 기준 첫 흑자는 2001년 4분기로 알려져 있으나 카드에는 연간 기준만 적었습니다.
2004년 주주서한의 "Our ultimate financial measure, and the one we most want to drive over the long-term, is free cash flow per share" 문구를 원문과 대조하세요. 카드에는 'ultimate financial measure'만 인용했습니다.
초기 Amazon이 재고를 적게 두고 상당수 책을 주문 후 도매상에서 조달했다는 내용은 1997년 투자설명서와 주주서한에서 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체적 수치 없이 질적으로만 적었습니다.
Amazon이 1998~1999년 전환사채 등으로 외부 자금도 조달했다는 내용(1번 판단 문제 C 피드백)을 10-K로 확인하세요.
3번 카드의 0일·20일·50일 타임라인은 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산: 재고 판매 20일 + 대금 회수 0일 − 공급업체 지불 50일 = −30일. Amazon의 실제 현금 전환 주기 일수는 연도별로 다르므로 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.
마켓플레이스 판매자 대금을 일정 주기로 지급한다는 내용은 Seller Central 안내로 확인하세요. 구체적 주기(예: 14일)는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: How Amazon's customers helped pay for its growth
body: Amazon went public in 1997 as an online bookstore. It didn't report a full-year profit until 2003.
Losing money while growing fast usually burns through cash. But Amazon had a quiet advantage: its customers often paid before Amazon paid its suppliers.

image.label: Parcels on a conveyor, coins flowing in ahead of them
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 컨베이어 벨트 위 택배 상자들, 상자보다 앞서 동전이 창고 안으로 흘러 들어오고, 공급업체로 나가는 동전은 멀리 뒤쪽에서 천천히 나감. 실제 Amazon 로고, 미소 화살표, 상자 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your board says: slow down to save cash.
body: It's the late 1990s. You run a fast-growing online bookstore. Customers pay by card when they order, and the money arrives within days. Your book suppliers bill you and expect payment weeks later.
You're reporting losses. A board member wants you to slow growth to protect cash. What do you do?

options.text: Agree. Losses plus fast growth will drain the bank
options.feedback: That's true for most businesses. Here, slowing down would shrink the customer cash arriving ahead of supplier bills, so it could actually hurt cash.

options.text: Keep growing, as long as customers keep paying before suppliers get paid
options.feedback: When cash comes in before it goes out, each extra sale adds money you hold for weeks. You still have to fix the losses, but growth isn't what's draining you.

options.text: Keep growing, but only after raising a large loan
options.feedback: A cushion is sensible, and Amazon did raise outside money too. But the loan costs interest, and it misses that your payment timing is already a source of cash.

cards.title: Follow one order.
body: Here the business holds the customer's money for **30 days** before it owes the supplier. The numbers are made up; the order of events is the point.

cards.title: A negative cash cycle
body: The **cash cycle** is the time between paying for what you sell and getting paid for it. Most businesses pay first and collect later, so they wait.

When customers pay before you pay suppliers, the cycle turns **negative**. You hold their money first. Fast-selling stock and card payments at checkout made this possible for Amazon from its early bookstore days.

image.label: Two timelines: cash out first vs cash in first
image.brief: 두 개의 가로 타임라인 비교. 위쪽 "Most businesses": 빨간 화살표(Pay supplier)가 먼저, 초록 화살표(Customer pays)가 나중, 사이에 "Waiting" 구간. 아래쪽 "Negative cash cycle": 초록이 먼저, 빨강이 나중, 사이에 "Cash you hold" 구간 강조.

cards.title: Growth makes the float bigger.
body: When sales rise every month, today's incoming customer cash is larger than the supplier bills from smaller, earlier months. So growth adds cash instead of eating it.

Amazon cared about this openly. In his 2004 shareholder letter, Jeff Bezos called free cash flow per share Amazon's "ultimate financial measure." Later, its marketplace worked the same way: Amazon collects from buyers and pays third-party sellers on a schedule, not instantly.
cards.softwareNote: Annual prepaid subscriptions create the same effect. A customer pays for twelve months up front, while servers and salaries are paid month by month. Growth in annual plans brings cash in ahead of the costs.

cards.title: The float runs in reverse.
body: That cash isn't yours. It's owed. If sales stop growing or start shrinking, you must pay large old supplier bills from smaller new sales, and cash drains fast.
It also doesn't fix losses. A negative cycle buys time, not profit. And pushing suppliers to wait ever longer has a cost: they may raise prices, cut service or walk away.

cards.title: Now it's a shelving factory.
body: You make custom steel shelving for warehouses. Steel suppliers want payment in 30 days. Production takes about three weeks. Customers pay 60 days after delivery.
A new client offers an order that would double your sales. How do you take it?

options.text: Accept and cover the gap with a bank overdraft
options.feedback: You win the order, but you pay interest on a gap that doubles with the order. If the client pays late, the overdraft grows with no limit in sight.

options.text: Accept, ask for a deposit at signing and longer steel terms
options.feedback: You move cash in earlier and cash out later, shrinking the gap that growth would create. You may give a small discount for the deposit, but you grow without betting the bank.

options.text: Decline. Doubling sales is too risky for cash
options.feedback: You protect today's cash but give up the growth. The problem is the payment timing, not the order, and timing can often be renegotiated.

cards.title: Who pays first decides whether growth feeds or drains you.
body: Amazon's early growth was partly funded by customers paying before suppliers were paid. Most businesses can't flip their cycle fully, but almost any can shorten it.
**Try it today:** for your main product, write down how many days pass between paying your supplier and getting paid by your customer. Pick one step to shorten by a week.
